text:
In ashen lands, greenless and scorched,
as I complained to Nature,
and the dagger of my mind, wandering at random,
slowly sharpened itself upon my heart,
a great dark cloud, born of a storm,
that housed a troop of vicious demons
like furious, cruel dwarfs,
turned then to stare coldly at me;
and, like travelers astonished by a madman,
I heard them laugh and whisper among themselves,
exchanging signs and knowing winks:

“Let us look at our leisure at this caricature,
this shade of Hamlet aping his pose,
hair in the wind, uncertain gaze.
Is it not truly pitiful to see such a reveler,
this scoundrel, idler, lazy actor,
who, because he plays his part with art,
expects, by singing of his woes, to interest
the eagle and the cricket, the brook and flowers,
and even us, authors of such columns,
by loudly declaiming his public tirades?”

I could have simply turned away
my sovereign head—my pride is high as mountains
and rules over demons and storm clouds—
had I not glimpsed among that filthy troop
—and this crime did not make the sun reel!—
the queen of my soul, she of the peerless gaze,
laughing with them at my dark affliction
and, in passing, offering them an obscene caress.

translation.title: Beatrice
translation.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Baudelaire. The theatrical mockery and the final betrayal by the speaker’s Beatrice are retained.
